claims.text: High-temperature stability of multi-element near-equiatomic nanoparticles is primarily governed by atomic-diffusion kinetics.
Rapid high-temperature synthesis can kinetically freeze a homogeneous, high-entropy elemental distribution in these nanoparticles.
Entropy-stabilized multi-element nanoparticles have reduced atomic diffusion because of high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics.
Reduced atomic diffusion preserves a uniform elemental distribution during thermal annealing.
A fully diffusion-equilibrated state exhibits clear elemental segregation, including segregation of Ru, Rh, and Ni in the cited MEA nanoparticles.
Longer dwell times or slower cooling enhance atomic mobility sufficiently to cause elemental segregation and phase separation.
Rapid heating and cooling preserve the kinetically trapped high-entropy state by limiting atomic mobility.
Slower thermal profiles allow diffusion to overcome entropy-associated diffusion barriers.
Elemental segregation causes structural and chemical instability.
Nanoparticles exposed to longer dwell times or slower cooling will show more compositional inhomogeneity and phase separation than rapidly annealed controls.
Increased segregation or phase separation will degrade catalytic or thermoelectric performance.
The standard rapid synthesis protocol yields a homogeneous, high-entropy metallic baseline state.
The rapidly processed baseline exhibits minimal diffusion-driven segregation under controlled annealing.
Diffusion-controlled stability is most critical in systems with low noble-metal content.
Extremely high cooling rates can suppress or mask diffusion-driven segregation.
Inherently low diffusion coefficients can mask the effect of thermal-profile changes.
The proposed mechanism applies across catalytic service temperatures of 773–1173 K and thermoelectric service temperatures of 473–1923 K.
Nanoparticle–support anchoring can independently provide excellent thermal stability.

A statistically significant absence of additional segregation, phase separation, and performance degradation in slow-profile samples relative to rapid-profile controls would falsify the proposed diffusion-dominant hypothesis.
